text: Socrates founds his city on need, and no idea of a city comes before it. No one is self-sufficient (Republic II, 369b), so the first citizens are a farmer, a builder, a weaver, and a shoemaker, each doing the one work his nature suits. A city that stayed at that size would never need a soldier. Glaucon refuses to live there. He wants couches and side dishes (372d–e), and Socrates grants him a "feverish" city. Appetite grows, and its growth ends in war: the land that fed the healthy city cannot feed the feverish one, so the city must take its neighbors' land and defend its own (373d–e). A class of warriors follows of necessity. With it comes the question that occupies the rest of the reading. What kind of person can be trusted with weapons? Socrates finds the answer in a well-bred dog, gentle to those it knows and fierce to strangers (375a–e). From the dog he draws the first of the city's many surprises. The guardian tells friend from enemy by knowledge, and so he is already a philosopher of a kind (376b).
